title: SQL Fundamentals
tagline: Data types, NULL and three-valued logic, DML & transactions, and query evaluation order

placementQuiz.q: A column holds whole numbers only and must never overflow on aggregates. Which type is the safe choice?
placementQuiz.explain: numeric is arbitrary-precision; int4/int8 overflow on big sums, float8 rounds.

placementQuiz.q: Which condition correctly matches rows where a nullable column is NULL?
placementQuiz.explain: NULL = anything yields NULL (unknown), so equality never matches; use IS NULL.

placementQuiz.q: In SQL's three-valued logic, which is TRUE?
placementQuiz.explain: OR TRUE short-circuits the unknown to TRUE; AND TRUE stays unknown.

placementQuiz.q: A multi-statement change must be fully reversible on an error. Which mechanism fits?
placementQuiz.explain: Wrap statements in BEGIN…COMMIT with SAVEPOINTs to roll back to a known point.

placementQuiz.q: You wrote SELECT amount * 1.1 AS gross … WHERE gross > 100. What's wrong?
options: Aliases in WHERE are illegal because filtering happens before SELECT
placementQuiz.explain: The logical order filters in WHERE before the SELECT computes aliases, so WHERE gross is undefined.

sections.title: The Contract — Types, NULL, Evaluation Order

blocks.md: **SQL's job is to transform data with clear contracts — types, NULL semantics, and the order of evaluation are that contract. Learn the domain, not the tuning.**

blocks.text: Type Families — the Engine Decides Comparisons

blocks.md: Every column has a type, and the type decides how values compare, sort, and aggregate. **Numeric**: `int4`/`int8` are fixed-width and can overflow on big sums; `numeric` is arbitrary-precision and the safe choice for money and totals; `float8`/`real` are approximate binary floats. **Character**: `text`/`varchar`/`char`. **Temporal**: `timestamp` (no zone), `timestamptz` (zone-aware), `interval`. **Logical**: `boolean`. Mixing types triggers implicit casts the engine picks for you — working explicitly is the contract that removes surprise.

blocks.label: type behavior in PostgreSQL
blocks.code:
-- Cast a text literal to a timestamp
SELECT '2024-01-15 10:30:00'::timestamp;

-- Integer division truncates in PostgreSQL
SELECT 7/2   AS int_division;      -- 3
SELECT 7.0/2 AS float_division;    -- 3.5

-- Binary floats are approximate
SELECT 0.1 + 0.2;                  -- 0.30000000000000004
blocks.pg:
-- Standard CAST() also works in PostgreSQL
SELECT CAST('2024-01-15 10:30:00' AS timestamp);
blocks.mysql:
-- MySQL has no :: syntax; use CAST(... AS ...)
SELECT CAST('2024-01-15 10:30:00' AS DATETIME);
-- 7 / 2 evaluates to 3.5000 in MySQL; DIV gives the integer part
SELECT 7 DIV 2; -- 3

blocks.label: explicit casts avoid ambiguity
blocks.code:
-- Two spellings of the same cast (PostgreSQL)
SELECT CAST('2024-01-15' AS date) AS via_standard,
       '2024-01-15'::date          AS via_colon_cast;

-- Comparing a text column to a date literal relies on an implicit
-- cast. It usually works, but be explicit:
SELECT * FROM products
WHERE  created_on = DATE '2024-01-15';
-- or: WHERE created_on = CAST('2024-01-15' AS date)
blocks.pg: -- DATE 'literal' is a typed literal cast in PostgreSQL

items.explain: Both operands are integers, so PostgreSQL truncates to 3; write 7.0/2 or CAST(7 AS numeric)/2 for a fractional result.

options: Numeric types round to 15 significant digits
Binary floats represent 0.1 and 0.2 only approximately
An implicit CAST to integer happened
Floating point division is exact by definition
items.explain: float8 is a binary fraction; 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary representation, so their sum is inexact. Use numeric for exact decimal arithmetic.

blocks.text: NULL Means Unknown — and Unknown Participates in Logic

blocks.md: NULL is **not** zero and not the empty string — it is *unknown*. Any comparison with NULL evaluates to a third truth value: UNKNOWN. `col = NULL` is never TRUE, so it never matches; filter with `IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL`. Aggregates mostly ignore NULLs, which is exactly why `count(*)` and `count(col)` can disagree.

blocks.label: equality vs IS NULL
blocks.pg:
-- PostgreSQL-only null-safe equality:
SELECT 5 IS NOT DISTINCT FROM NULL;      -- false
SELECT NULL IS NOT DISTINCT FROM NULL;   -- true
blocks.mysql:
-- MySQL uses the <=> null-safe equal operator instead:
SELECT NULL <=> NULL;  -- 1
SELECT 5 <=> NULL;     -- 0

blocks.label: coalesce, nullif, counting
blocks.code:
-- Supply a fallback for NULL
SELECT COALESCE(NULL, 'default');   -- 'default'

-- NULLIF(a, b) returns NULL when a = b, otherwise a
SELECT NULLIF(5, 5), NULLIF(5, 6);  -- NULL, 5

-- count(*) counts rows; count(email) counts non-NULL emails
SELECT count(*)      AS all_rows,
       count(email)  AS with_email
FROM   users;
blocks.pg: -- count(col) ignores NULLs; count(*) never ignores rows
blocks.mysql: -- Same semantics in MySQL 8.0; '' is a value there, NULL is separate

blocks.label: three-valued logic truth tables
blocks.code:
-- AND truth table (x AND y)
--   x\y   T      F      N
--   T     T      F      N
--   F     F      F      F
--   N     N      F      N

-- OR truth table (x OR y)
--   x\y   T      F      N
--   T     T      T      T
--   F     T      F      N
--   N     T      N      N

-- T or F is enough to decide; N only flips results it cannot resolve.
blocks.pg: -- NULL = the UNKNOWN truth value in PostgreSQL's three-valued logic
blocks.mysql: -- MySQL follows the same truth tables for the boolean NULL

items.q: count(*) returns 100 rows but count(email) returns 80. Why?
options: Some rows duplicate an email value
20 rows have NULL in the email column
The table has 20 rows deleted by a trigger
items.explain: count(*) counts every row; count(email) skips NULLs, so the 20-row gap means 20 NULL emails.

items.q: Which query returns rows whose middle_initial is NULL?
items.explain: Only IS NULL (or IS NOT DISTINCT FROM NULL) can match NULL; all comparisons against NULL yield UNKNOWN.

blocks.text: INSERT / UPDATE / DELETE and All-or-Nothing Transactions

blocks.label: insert with returning
blocks.code:
-- RETURNING hands back the generated key in the same statement
INSERT INTO products (name, price)
VALUES ('T-Shirt', 19.99)
RETURNING id;

blocks.label: update
blocks.pg: -- Standard UPDATE; RETURNING shows the new row
blocks.mysql: -- Same statement in MySQL 8.0; multi-table UPDATE only joins extra tables

blocks.label: transaction with savepoints
blocks.code:
BEGIN;

INSERT INTO orders (user_id) VALUES (42);

SAVEPOINT p1;                            -- mark a safe point

UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1
WHERE  sku = 'TS1';                     -- unwanted or failed step

ROLLBACK TO p1;                         -- undo ONLY the update

COMMIT;                                 -- commit the remaining INSERT
blocks.pg:
-- SAVEPOINT / ROLLBACK TO / RELEASE are SQL-standard and fully
-- supported in PostgreSQL; a savepoint may overlap and nest
blocks.mysql:
-- MySQL 8.0 supports SAVEPOINT and ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT inside
-- transactions started with START TRANSACTION

blocks.md: **Atomicity:** a transaction commits all of its statements or none. `ROLLBACK TO p1` unwinds work performed after the savepoint *without* aborting the whole transaction, so the earlier `INSERT` can still commit. This is the tool for partial-recovery flows.

items.q: After ROLLBACK TO p1;, what state is the transaction in?
options: Aborted and closed — nothing can commit
Statements after p1 are undone; the transaction stays open and COMMIT still works
The entire transaction is rolled back to BEGIN
items.explain: ROLLBACK TO returns to the savepoint, discarding later work, and the transaction remains usable.

blocks.label: logical processing order
blocks.code:
-- SQL's documented logical order (a contract, not an execution plan)
--  1. FROM        build the row source(s)
--  2. WHERE       filter individual rows
--  3. GROUP BY    form groups
--  4. HAVING      filter groups (aggregates allowed)
--  5. SELECT      compute output expressions and aliases
--  6. ORDER BY    final ordering
--
-- Real engines optimize aggressively and may physically reorder;
-- the clause order above is the logical contract that defines what
-- each clause is allowed to reference.
blocks.pg: -- PostgreSQL's planner may reorder freely as long as the result matches
blocks.mysql: -- MySQL 8.0 honors the same logical contract

blocks.label: where vs having
blocks.code:
SELECT dept, count(*) AS n
FROM   emp
WHERE  salary > 3000       -- filters rows BEFORE grouping
GROUP  BY dept
HAVING count(*) > 5       -- filters groups AFTER aggregation
ORDER  BY n DESC;
blocks.pg: -- WHERE cannot reference count(*); HAVING can

blocks.md: `WHERE` runs before grouping and can never reference aggregates. `HAVING` runs after grouping and can. The same reasoning explains why a `SELECT` alias is invisible in `WHERE` (aliases are computed last) yet perfectly legal in `ORDER BY`.

items.q: Which clause may reference an aggregate such as count(*)?
items.explain: HAVING runs after grouping, so it can test aggregate values; WHERE sees only raw input rows.

blocks.md: **Reading the plan:** the `Filter: (salary > 3000)` sits on the Seq Scan — rows are discarded before any grouping — then `GroupAggregate` forms groups by `dept` and drops groups via its own `Filter: (count(*) > 5)`. That is the WHERE-before-HAVING contract, visible in the tree.

blocks.sql:
SELECT CAST('2024-01-15' AS DATE);
SELECT CURRENT_DATE;

-- NULL is UNKNOWN everywhere
SELECT * FROM t WHERE col IS NULL;
blocks.pg:
SELECT NULL = NULL;    -- NULL (UNKNOWN)
SELECT NULL IS NULL;   -- true
-- NULLs sort LAST in ASC order by default
blocks.mysql:
SELECT NULL <=> NULL;  -- 1 (null-safe)
SELECT '' IS NULL;     -- 0: empty string is a value, not NULL
-- NULLs sort FIRST in ASC order by default

blocks.subtitle: Synthetic drills to lock in types, NULL logic, transactions and evaluation order.

items.title: Fix the Implicit-Cast Bug
items.statement: A table stores timestamps as text. `WHERE created = '2024-01-15'` silently misses rows whose stored value is '2024-01-15 10:30:00'. Explain why, then fix it with an explicit cast.
hints: The comparison is text = text: '2024-01-15' does not equal '2024-01-15 10:30:00' as a string
Use CAST(created AS timestamp) with a typed boundary, or store a real timestamptz column

items.title: NULL Equality Trap
items.statement: `SELECT * FROM users WHERE deactivated_at = NULL;` returns zero rows even though deactivated users exist. Fix the predicate and explain why the original matches nothing.
hints: NULL = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN, which WHERE rejects
Use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL

items.title: Truth-Table Reasoning
items.statement: Classify each expression as TRUE, FALSE, or UNKNOWN: NULL AND TRUE, NULL OR TRUE, NULL AND FALSE, NOT NULL. Which single one is TRUE, and why?

items.title: Transaction with Savepoints
items.statement: In one transaction: insert an order, mark a savepoint, update stock for sku 'TS1', then decide the stock update was wrong and roll back only that statement while still committing the insert. Write the statements in order.
hints: BEGIN; ... INSERT ...; SAVEPOINT p1; UPDATE ...; ROLLBACK TO p1; COMMIT;
ROLLBACK TO keeps the transaction alive; only the post-savepoint work is undone

items.title: COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col)
items.statement: On one table, count(*) returns 1,000 but count(phone) returns 940. Explain the discrepancy and write the query that reports both numbers side by side.
hints: count(phone) skips NULLs; count(*) counts every row
SELECT count(*) AS total, count(phone) AS with_phone FROM t;

items.title: Alias-in-WHERE Ordering Bug
items.statement: SELECT amount * 1.1 AS gross FROM invoice WHERE gross > 100; refuses or misbehaves. Diagnose it against the logical evaluation order and produce a working query with the same intent.
hints: SELECT aliases are computed after WHERE, so WHERE gross cannot see the alias
Recompute the predicate: WHERE amount * 1.1 > 100 — or wrap it: SELECT * FROM (SELECT amount * 1.1 AS gross FROM invoice) t WHERE gross > 100;

revisionCard: 7/2 truncates to 3 in PostgreSQL; 7.0/2 is 3.5 — the operands' types decide
3VL: NULL compared with anything is UNKNOWN; only IS NULL / IS NOT NULL (or IS NOT DISTINCT FROM) match NULL
count(*) counts rows; count(col) skips NULLs
Logical order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY — WHERE can't see aliases or aggregates, HAVING can
SAVEPOINT / ROLLBACK TO / RELEASE let a transaction recover part-way without aborting
Always cast comparisons explicitly — implicit casts are a silent surprise

glossary.def: Truth system with TRUE, FALSE, UNKNOWN; comparisons involving NULL yield UNKNOWN.
Automatic type conversion the engine picks when an expression's type differs from the context.
Named marker inside a transaction; ROLLBACK TO returns to it without aborting the transaction.
A transaction commits all of its changes or none; partial success is impossible.
Matching NULL values with IS NULL / IS NOT NULL instead of = or <>.
SQL's documented logical clause order (FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY) that defines what each clause may reference.
